alt: A two-by-two grid of formal and informal control against positive and negative sanctions: a bravery award is formal positive, a court sentence formal negative, a parent’s praise informal positive and being ignored by friends informal negative. A note explains that internalised control is the strongest.
caption: Sanctions can be formal or informal, positive or negative.

alt: A table of five formal agencies, government, police, courts, penal system and armed forces, with their main methods and when they are more or less effective. A note explains that coercion is a last resort and that conformity through fear is less stable.
caption: Formal control works best when people see the rules and penalties as legitimate.

alt: Plan of a panopticon: a ring of cells around a central watchtower. Because prisoners could not tell when a guard was looking, they behaved as though always observed. Digital surveillance such as CCTV, facial recognition, number-plate cameras and phone location data works the same way; critics raise privacy and misuse.
caption: Knowing you might be watched changes behaviour.

alt: A table of six informal agencies with their positive and negative sanctions, from parental treats and grounding to promotion and dismissal. Below: informal control is usually more effective because it is constant, but weaker in anonymous cities and among people who do not care about approval.
caption: Informal control draws its power from relationships people value.

alt: Functionalism sees control protecting shared values, with Durkheim’s idea that punishment unites society. Marxism sees it serving the ruling class; Althusser separates repressive state apparatuses that use force from ideological ones that persuade. Feminism, through Heidensohn, sees control maintaining patriarchy at home, in public and at work.
caption: One consensus view and two conflict views of who benefits from control.

alt: Deviant behaviour breaks norms; non-conformist behaviour rejects expectations without breaking the law. Four kinds of resistance: protest groups such as the school climate strikes, youth subcultures such as punk, online subcultures and religious subcultures. Reasons for joining include belonging, grievances, status, excitement and friends.
caption: Subcultures resist mainstream control but usually impose strong control of their own.

alt: A balance weighing conflict arguments that control benefits the powerful, from Marxists and Heidensohn, against consensus arguments that it benefits everyone, such as laws against violence and Durkheim’s view of punishment. It tips slightly towards the conflict side, and the judgement says the powerful benefit more.
caption: Set conflict against consensus, then reach a judgement.
